questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit at Infinity of a Power Function With an Even Power
questions.worked_solution:
First note that $ln⁡(0.9)<0.$

The graph $y={x}^{4}$ looks like an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{4}=\infty .
$$

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient $ln⁡(0.9)$ causes $y=ln⁡(0.9)\cdot {x}^{4}$ to look more like a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(ln⁡(0.9)\cdot {x}^{4})=-{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{4})=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

The figure above shows the graph of $f(x).$ Find ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Applying the product rule and the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot ({lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{({lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x))}\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }f(x)=3.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{f(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{3}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{2}$ is an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }{x}^{2}=\infty .
$$

Multiplication by the positive constant $\frac{1}{3}$ does not change the sign of the limit. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2})={lim}_{x\to -\infty }({x}^{2})=\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{6}{(f(x))}^{1/5}) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{6}\cdot \sqrt[5]{f(x)}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt[5]{f(x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}\cdot \sqrt[5]{{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x)=-32.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{6}{(f(x))}^{1/5}) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}\cdot \sqrt[5]{-32} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}\cdot (-2) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }-2{x}^{6} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $y={x}^{6}$ looks similar to an upward parabola, so

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{6}=\infty .
$$

However, multiplying by the negative coefficient $-2$ causes $y=-2{x}^{6}$ to look more like a downward parabola. This changes the sign of the limit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }(-2{x}^{6})=-{lim}_{x\to \infty }({x}^{6})=-\infty .\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Given that $p(x)={x}^{2}$ and $q(x)=-7{x}^{4},$ what is ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot p(x)}{q(x)}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's calculate ${x}^{2}\cdot p(x):$

$$
{x}^{2}\cdot p(x)={x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}={x}^{4}.
$$

When we divide the two functions ${x}^{2}\cdot p(x)$ and $q(x),$ we get a constant, and the limit of a constant is just the constant itself:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}\cdot p(x)}{q(x)} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{4}}{(-7{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }-\frac{1}{7} \\  & =-\frac{1}{7}\end{aligned}
$$
